item.title: VS Code extension enables Python in Web via WebAssembly
item.description:
VS Code extension enables Python in Web via WebAssembly

A new VS Code extension allows users to run Python code in the Web, such as in vscode.dev, using WebAssembly as the execution engine. The project is designed primarily as an experimentation environment to help the VS Code team gain experience with running Python code in the Web using WebAssembly technologies.

🧩 How it works

The extension utilizes a pre-configured Python environment based on CPython WebAssembly builds, specifically the Python-3.11.0rc1-wasm32-wasi-16.zip build. It depends on the GitHub Repositories extension and requires users to authenticate with GitHub.

Users can set up their own Python environment, including source wheel Python packages, by following these steps:

  • Create a new GitHub repository.
  • Download a wasm-wasi-16 build from the tiran/cpython-wasm-test releases and expand it into the root of the repository.
  • To add source wheel packages, create a site-packages folder in the root.
  • Install the package using the command pip install my_package --target ./site-packages (requires a local Python installation with pip).
  • Commit the changes.
  • Change the python.wasm.runtime setting to point to the user’s GitHub repository.

⚙️ Key details

The extension is not intended for productive Python development due to several limitations:

  • No pip support.
  • No socket support.
  • No support for native Python modules.
  • No thread support.
  • No async support, as a consequence of the lack of thread support.

Regarding versioning, odd major, minor, or patch version numbers indicate an insider or pre-release. For example, 1.0.0 and 0.1.0 are pre-releases, while 2.0.2 is a regular release. The initial version was 0.5.0, and version 0.7.0 added basic debugging support.

💡 Why it matters

This project serves as a testbed for integrating WebAssembly with Python in web-based development environments. It also outlines contribution requirements, noting that most contributions require agreeing to a Contributor License Agreement (CLA) to grant rights to use the contribution.

#VSCode #WebAssembly #Python #Extension

Source: microsoft/vscode-python-web-wasm

Roo Code Extension Launches 225-Agent Configuration Library for 2026 Standards

Roo Code has released a professional AI agent configuration library featuring 225 specialized agents for VS Code. This update provides enhanced AI coding assistance configurations aligned with modern software development principles.

🧩 How it works

The repository contains a meticulously curated collection of YAML-based configurations designed to accelerate development workflows. Each agent is optimized for 2026 development standards, utilizing a modular architecture that supports cross-platform compatibility. The system includes production-ready templates that allow for easy customization through YAML files.

⚙️ Key details

item.title: GitHub Actions extension allows local workflow testing in VS Code
item.description:
GitHub Actions extension allows local workflow testing in VS Code

The GitHub Local Actions Visual Studio Code extension is now available, enabling developers to run and test GitHub Actions workflows locally without leaving their editor. This tool leverages the act tool to execute the set of actions defined in .github/workflows/ files by using Docker to pull or build necessary images and run containers for each action.

💡 Why it matters

  • Fast Feedback: Instead of committing and pushing changes to test modifications to .github/workflows/ files, developers can use act to run actions locally.
  • Local Task Runner: The extension allows GitHub Actions to replace Makefile functionality, addressing the need to avoid repeating tasks.
  • Environment Parity: The environment variables and filesystem are configured to match what GitHub provides for hosted runners.

🧩 How it works

When act is executed, it reads GitHub Actions from the .github/workflows/ directory and determines the execution path based on defined dependencies. The process involves:

  • Using the Docker API to pull or build necessary images as defined in workflow files.
  • Running containers for each action based on the prepared images.
  • Matching environment variables and filesystem configurations to GitHub’s standards.

⚙️ Key details

  • Documentation: The act user guide is available at nektosact.com.
  • Community Support: Users can ask for help in the project’s discussions section on GitHub.
  • Contributing: Developers can contribute by following the guidelines found in the CONTRIBUTING.md file.
  • Development Requirements: Building and installing the tool requires Go (version 1.26.0) and Docker. Unit tests are run via make test, while fast tests without Docker use make test-fast.

#GitHubActions #VSCode #DevOps #Docker #act

Source: nektos/act

item.title: GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions
item.description:
GitHub develops Agent Host Protocol to enable continuous multi-device AI sessions

The newly developed Agent Host Protocol (AHP) is an open standard designed to keep AI agent sessions accessible and continuous across editors, applications, mobile phones, and the cloud. As models become capable of working independently for hours or days, AHP ensures that developers can check in on their progress from any device, allowing sessions to persist even when users switch devices or close windows.

🔍 Overview

In the past, GitHub Copilot was built as a VS Code extension, tying the lifetime of agents directly to the VS Code editor window. Closing the window, restarting VS Code for an update, or connecting to a remote machine would terminate the agent session or reset the extension host. To resolve this limitation and allow developers to pull agents into their custom workflows, editors, terminals, or mobile apps, the Agent Host Protocol provides a standard, independently versioned language. This shared protocol ensures every client sees the same agents, history, and state without requiring bespoke, one-off integrations.

🧩 How it works

To handle multi-client interactions seamlessly, the Agent Host Protocol is designed with several core architectural features:

  • URI-identified Channels: This is the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, and can optionally implement other channels such as terminal support, Model Context Protocol (MCP) additions, or OpenTelemetry (OTel) reporting.
  • Reducer-Based State Object: Inside each channel, a reducer-based state object drives client-side logic. The server acts as the arbiter of this state, while the client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects.
  • Network Resiliency: Under poor network conditions, reconnection and replay are simplified. Clients can send all queued actions and present a loading state while waiting for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions.
  • Minimal Core: To make implementation straightforward on custom clients and servers, the core protocol is kept minimal while allowing extensive features to be built on top.

⚙️ Key details

  • Focus on Interaction, Not Behavior: Unlike the Language Server Protocol (LSP) or Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP), AHP avoids encoding how agents work, focusing solely on how users interact with them to accommodate rapidly evolving agent models.
  • Rebuilding the VS Code Stack: Adopting AHP in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The existing Copilot Chat extension had grown for over three years to more than 400,000 lines of TypeScript (excluding tests) and was heavily dependent on the VS Code window lifecycle and APIs that are unavailable in a standalone agent host process.

#AHP #GitHubCopilot #AIAgents #VSCode #DeveloperTools

Source: Building the Agent Host Protocol for sessions that continue across devices

item.title: 🚀 VS Code Revolution: How GitHub Copilot Is Going Open Source
item.description:
🚀 VS Code Revolution: How GitHub Copilot Is Going Open Source

Summary: VS Code is making a groundbreaking move by open-sourcing GitHub Copilot Chat components and integrating core AI capabilities directly into VS Code. This article explores what this means for developers, why Microsoft is making this strategic shift, and how you can prepare to take advantage of these powerful AI features when they arrive in 2025.

🌟 The Unexpected AI Evolution: VS Code’s Bold New Direction

In a stunning announcement that has reverberated across the developer community, the VS Code team revealed plans to transform their beloved editor into an “Open Source AI Editor.” 🤯 This isn’t just another feature update—it’s a fundamental shift in philosophy concerning how AI-powered development tools should be built, maintained, and evolved.

On May 19, 2025, through their official blog post “VS Code: Open Source AI Editor,” the team outlined their vision: GitHub Copilot Chat extension code will be open-sourced under the MIT license, with key AI components being thoughtfully refactored into VS Code’s core functionality.

Why does this matter? Because for many developers, AI coding assistants have become essential productivity tools—but they’ve largely existed as closed-source, premium add-ons. This move signals a future where AI assistance becomes as fundamental to coding as syntax highlighting or code completion.

📸 Imagine a screenshot showing the evolution of code editors from simple text editors to intelligent coding assistants

🧠 The Strategic Rationale: Why Open Source AI Now?

The VS Code team’s decision wasn’t made lightly. After all, GitHub Copilot has been tremendously successful as a premium offering. So what changed?

1. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗟𝗟𝗠 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗲 𝗛𝗮𝘀 𝗘𝘃𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝗱

Large Language Models have matured significantly. The “secret sauce” of prompt engineering that once gave proprietary systems their edge has diminished in importance as models themselves have become more capable. The team recognized this shift makes now the perfect time to open the ecosystem.

2. 𝙐𝙨𝙚𝙧 𝙀𝙭𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙘𝙚 𝙋𝙖𝙩𝙩𝙚𝙧𝙣𝙨 𝙃𝙖𝙫𝙚 𝙎𝙩𝙖𝙗𝙞𝙡𝙞𝙯𝙚𝙙

Common patterns for effective AI-human interaction in coding environments have emerged. By open-sourcing these patterns, VS Code provides a stable foundation that the community can build upon, rather than having everyone reinvent the UI wheel.

3. 𝑇𝑟𝑎𝑛𝑠𝑝𝑎𝑟𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑦 & 𝑆𝑒𝑐𝑢𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑦 𝐷𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑𝑠

As AI tools become more integrated into development workflows, questions about data collection and security vulnerabilities have intensified. Open-sourcing addresses these concerns head-on by allowing developers to see exactly what data is being collected and how it’s used. Security benefits too, as more eyes on the code means faster identification and remediation of potential vulnerabilities.

“𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘑𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘺 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘊𝘭𝘰𝘴𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘖𝘱𝘦𝘯 𝘐𝘴 𝘈𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘌𝘮𝘱𝘰𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘊𝘰𝘮𝘮𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘺”

🔧 Getting Ready: How to Prepare for the Open Source AI Revolution

Since these AI features will be integrated into VS Code itself rather than offered as a separate “open-source Copilot,” you’ll want to ensure you’re using the latest version of VS Code when these features roll out. Here’s a quick setup guide for different platforms:

🪟 Windows Setup:

  1. Download the installer from the official VS Code website (code.visualstudio.com)
  2. Run the installer and activate the “Add to PATH” option
  3. Consider enabling helpful context menu features like “Open with Code”

🍏 macOS Setup:

  1. Download the Universal .zip file from the official site
  2. Extract and drag Visual Studio Code.app to your Applications folder
  3. To enable terminal access, open VS Code, press Cmd+Shift+P, and type “Shell Command: Install ‘code’ command in PATH”

🐧 Linux Setup:

Options include:

  • For Debian-based systems: Download and install the .deb package
  • For RHEL/Fedora: Use the .rpm package
  • For various distributions: sudo snap install --classic code

📸 Visualize a simple setup diagram showing VS Code installation across different operating systems

The most important preparation step is staying informed. Keep an eye on the VS Code blog and release notes for announcements about when these AI features will be integrated. Regular updates will ensure you’re ready when they arrive.

🔮 The Implications: What This Means for the Developer Ecosystem

This shift isn’t just about making one product’s features freely available. It represents a fundamental transformation in how we think about AI-assisted development tools. By creating an open foundation for AI coding assistance, VS Code is enabling:

  1. 🧩 Specialized Domain Adaptations: Community contributors can tailor AI capabilities for specific languages, frameworks, or domains

  2. 📚 Enhanced Educational Tools: More accessible AI coding tools will revolutionize how programming is taught and learned

  3. 🛠️ Innovative Coding Workflows: New development paradigms will emerge as developers experiment with and extend these AI capabilities

  4. 🔍 Greater Transparency: Developers can inspect exactly how these tools work, building trust in AI-assisted development

The most exciting aspect is that this transformation puts the community at the center of AI-assisted development’s future. Rather than passive consumers of proprietary AI features, developers become active participants in shaping how these tools evolve.

🌐 Conclusion: A New Chapter in Development History

VS Code’s decision to open-source GitHub Copilot Chat components and integrate AI capabilities into its core represents more than just a feature announcement—it’s a philosophical statement about the future of development.

By applying the time-tested principles of open source to cutting-edge AI, VS Code is betting that community collaboration will produce better, more trustworthy AI coding tools than closed systems can. Given open source’s track record of success, this seems like a wise bet.

As developers, we now have the opportunity to shape this exciting future. When these changes roll out, will you simply use these new AI features, or will you contribute to building them?

What kind of AI-powered development environment do you want to create?
